questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from 'xyrk yksgk' where the outcome is the opposite of what the characters or reader expect.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when events turn out contrary to what is expected or appropriate. In the story, Èkujke receives modern education and claims progressive values, yet he treats Eksgu exactly as his feudal father does — expecting servitude without dignity. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing it with verbal irony or citing a mere unfortunate event) reveals the student cannot distinguish between types of irony or link the device to the story's caste critique.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the 'laVh' (stone slab) functions as a symbol rather than just a setting detail. What abstract idea does it embody?
questions.a: The laVh is not merely a physical stone; it embodies the immovable, crushing weight of the caste system that pins Eksgu down even in death. When Eksgu dies leaning against it, the slab becomes a monument to systemic oppression. A wrong answer that describes it only as 'where he sat' shows the student misses the symbolic leap from concrete object to abstract theme — a core Class 11 analytical skill.

questions.q: Apply the concept of dramatic irony to the scene where the Thakur says Eksgu will one day become a big officer. Identify what the reader knows that the Thakur does not, and state the effect on the reader.
questions.a: The reader knows Eksgu's caste and the Thakur's true exploitative nature make social mobility impossible; the Thakur's words are hollow patronage. This dramatic irony deepens the reader's outrage at the hypocrisy. A wrong answer that misses the reader's superior knowledge or the hypocrisy indicates the student cannot operationalize dramatic irony beyond definition.

questions.q: Analyze how the symbol of 'ikuh' (sugarcane) and its crushing operate at two levels: literal agricultural process and metaphorical social process. Connect both levels to the theme of exploitation.
questions.a: Literally, sugarcane is crushed to extract juice for profit; metaphorically, Eksgu's labor and body are crushed to extract value for the Thakur. The parallel is exact: both processes discard the residue (bagasse / human dignity) once utility is exhausted. A weak answer treats them as separate images without showing the structural analogy, revealing an inability to trace sustained symbolism across the narrative.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's choice to end the story with the Thakur's only concern being 'who will do the work now?' rather than grief. Is this verbal irony, situational irony, or both? Justify your judgment.
questions.a: It is primarily situational irony: the expectation of human mourning is replaced by economic calculation. It also carries verbal irony if the Thakur's earlier 'care' is recalled — his words meant nothing. A student who labels it only 'sad' or 'cruel' without naming the irony type fails to demonstrate the precise terminology and evaluative reasoning the board demands.

questions.q: Create a new symbolic object for a short scene where a marginalized student enters an elite school. Describe the object, what it represents, and how you would use it to show irony in one paragraph.
questions.a: A polished brass nameplate on the student's desk that reads 'Scholar' but is cold to the touch — symbolizing institutional inclusion without warmth. Irony: the nameplate promises belonging, but the cold metal mirrors the peer group's indifference. A poor answer offers a generic object without dual literal/symbolic function or fails to embed irony, showing the student cannot synthesize device and theme creatively.
